title: Sympathetic Ophthalmia: The Ocular Duel
summary: A rare, sight-threatening bilateral granulomatous panuveitis occurring after penetrating ocular trauma or intraocular surgery. It represents a delayed T-cell mediated autoimmune response against uveoretinal self-antigens, leading to devastating inflammation in both the 'exciting' and 'sympathizing' eye.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Sympathetic Ophthalmia (SO) is a rare, bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that follows accidental or surgical penetrating trauma to one eye (the 'exciting' eye). The non-injured eye (the 'sympathizing' eye) subsequently develops inflammation. Historically associated with battlefield trauma, modern cases are frequently associated with multiple intraocular surgeries, particularly vitreoretinal procedures.

sections.title: Etiology: The Trigger Events
content: Accidental Penetrating Trauma: Historically the most common cause (60-70%).
Intraocular Surgery: Now accounts for ~30% of cases; Vitrectomy is the leading surgical cause.
Cataract extraction, evisceration (rarely), and even Nd:YAG cyclophotocoagulation.
Interval: Usually occurs within 3 months of injury (80%), but can range from days to decades.

branches: Sensitization: Uveoretinal antigens (S-antigen, Rhodopsin) released into lymphatics
Type IV Hypersensitivity: Delayed T-cell mediated response
MHC Class II Association: HLA-DR4, HLA-DRB1*04, and HLA-DQA1*03
Granulomatous Reaction: Non-necrotizing infiltration of uveal tract

rows: Uveal Infiltration
Diffuse, 'non-necrotizing' granulomatous infiltration of choroid with lymphocytes & epithelioid cells.
Choriocapillaris Sparing
Relative sparing of the choriocapillaris (distinguishes from VKH).
Dalen-Fuchs Nodules
Clusters of epithelioid cells, macrophages, and RPE cells located between RPE and Bruch's membrane.
Retinal Involvement
Usually spared except for perivascular cuffing and edema.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: Symptoms
content: Sympathizing Eye: Earliest sign is often 'blurring at near' (loss of accommodation).
Photophobia and mild redness.
Floating spots and decreased visual acuity.
Exciting Eye: Sudden worsening of chronic low-grade inflammation.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Anterior Segment: 'Mutton-fat' Keratic Precipitates (KPs), Koeppe/Busacca nodules, and posterior synechiae.
Vitreous: Significant vitritis (cells and haze).
Posterior Segment: Diffuse choroidal thickening, exudative retinal detachment.
Dalen-Fuchs Nodules: Multiple yellow-white mid-peripheral lesions.

rows: FFA (Early)
Multiple fluorescent 'pinpoint' leaks at the RPE level (starry sky appearance).
FFA (Late)
Late pooling of dye in areas of exudative RD; staining of the optic disc.
ICGA
Multiple hypofluorescent spots (more sensitive for choroidal involvement than FFA).
EDI-OCT
Significant choroidal thickening; subretinal fluid; bacillary layer detachment.
B-Scan USG
Diffuse thickening of the choroid without extrascleral extension.
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH)
No history of trauma; associated with exudative RD, hearing loss, and vitiligo; Choriocapillaris involved.
Sarcoidosis
Systemic involvement (lungs, hilar nodes); positive ACE/Lysozyme levels.
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada
Bilateral, but has no traumatic trigger.
Endophthalmitis
Acute onset, intense pain, hypopyon, often bacterial/fungal markers present.
Multifocal Choroiditis
Smaller lesions, typically seen in myopic females.

sections.title: Surgical Prevention & Timing
content: Step 1: Primary repair of the penetrating injury (maintain globe integrity).
Step 2: Assess visual potential. If the eye is blind (NPL), consider enucleation.
Step 3: The 'Golden Period' — Enucleation within 10-14 days of trauma is historically considered protective.
Step 4: Once inflammation starts in the sympathizing eye, enucleation of the exciting eye is controversial and may not help.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Initial Pulse: IV Methylprednisolone 1g/day for 3 days if severe.
High Dose Steroids: Oral Prednisolone 1.0–1.5 mg/kg/day, tapered slowly over 6-12 months.
Steroid Sparing: Early introduction of IMT (Immunomodulatory Therapy) if steroids fail or for long-term control.
Maintenance: Maintain on lowest effective dose to prevent relapse.

sections.title: Immunomodulatory Therapy (IMT)
content: Antimetabolites: Azathioprine (2mg/kg) or Mycophenolate Mofetil (1g BD).
Calcineurin Inhibitors: Cyclosporine A or Tacrolimus.
Biologics: Infliximab or Adalimumab (Anti-TNF alpha) for refractory cases.
Alkylating Agents: Chlorambucil or Cyclophosphamide (reserved for severe, resistant cases).

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Sudden loss of accommodation in a patient with history of ocular trauma.
New onset 'floaters' in the healthy eye post-surgery.
Non-compliance with steroid taper (leading to rebound inflammation).
Signs of Enucleation Delay beyond the 2-week window in a non-salvageable eye.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Complications: Complicated Cataract, Secondary Glaucoma, Macular Edema, Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV).
Prognosis: Historically poor, but with modern IMT, >75% of patients achieve 20/40 or better vision.
Recurrence: Relapses are common if steroids are tapered too rapidly.

sections.title: The Enucleation vs. Evisceration Debate
sections.content: Traditionally, enucleation was mandatory to prevent SO, as evisceration might leave residual uveal antigens. However, modern studies (including meta-analyses) suggest that the risk of SO after evisceration is extremely low (comparable to enucleation), leading many surgeons to prefer evisceration for better cosmetic outcomes in NPL eyes.

content.explanation: P: Pinpoint leaks on FFA; E: Exciting eye was the injured one; A: Antigens (uveoretinal) are the cause; R: Rare since modern microsurgery; L: Long-term steroids/IMT required; S: Sparing of Choriocapillaris.
